rows: [Margin, p. 285: Nodus III. Motum ab aeterno non extitisse.]
[Margin, p. 285: Knot III. That motion has not existed from eternity.]

Ereu. Rem magnam postulas, sed tam aequam, ut quantum in me situm est, eam efficere prorsus debeam. Et de motu quidem expeditior est quaestio. Quod enim hesterno colloquio de mundi infinitate digessimus, applicatione tantummodo indiget, & confecta res erit. A signo enim in quo sumus aliquam horam infinitis mediis absistere necessum est, eam, si nostris similis est, determinatam esse quoad existentiam & individualitatem, & inter duas aeque determinatas, unam priorem, posteriorem alteram esse collocatam. Inter hanc proinde & eam quae nunc (dum loquimur) praeterit invida, quomodo non sit inclusum quod volunt infinitum, Ego prorsus hebesco, & tam mihi clarescere sic futurum quam solem in meridie certus affirmo.

Ereu. A great thing you ask [postulas], but so fair, that, as far as is placed [situm est] in me, I ought entirely [prorsus] to accomplish it. And concerning motion indeed the question is readier [expeditior]. For what in yesterday’s conversation about the infinity of the world we digested [digessimus], needs only application, and the thing will be concluded [confecta]. For [on their view] it is necessary [necessum est] that some hour stand off [absistere] from the sign [signo] in which we are by infinite middles [mediis]; that it, if it is like ours, is determinate as to existence and individuality [individualitatem]; and that between two equally determinate [hours] one is placed prior, the other posterior. Between this [hour] therefore and that which now (while we speak) passes by, envious [invida], how that which they will [volunt] [to be] infinite should not be enclosed [inclusum], I am entirely dull [hebesco]; and I, certain, affirm that it grows as clear [clarescere] to me that it will be so, as the sun at midday.
Asphal. Hanc partem hesterno opere claram reddidisti; ad alteram itaque, si placet Andabatae, te converte.
Asphal. This part you rendered clear by yesterday’s work; to the other, therefore, if it pleases Andabata, turn yourself.

Andab. Mihi vero stomachus nescio quomodo seu volutatur seu nauseat, dum evomenda est tot annis radicata de tempore imaginario sententia; sed dum quaero quid cum ratione possim opponere, subito residet ille tumor & in placorem redit. Pergere proinde, si libet, per me licet.

Andab. To me indeed the stomach, I know not how, either rolls [volutatur] or is nauseated, while the opinion [sententia] concerning imaginary time, rooted for so many years, is to be vomited out; but while I seek what I could oppose with reason [cum ratione], suddenly that swelling [tumor] settles and returns into calm [placorem]. To proceed, therefore, if it pleases [libet], is permitted as far as I am concerned [per me licet].
Ereu. Hoc ergo dic quid censeas: num corpus aliquod in signo praesenti existens, possit in eodem hoc signo non esse? Et loquor de compositione in re, non in mente.

Ereu. Say, therefore, what you judge [censeas] of this: whether some body existing in the present sign [signo] can in this same sign not be? And I speak of composition [compositione] in the thing [in re], not in the mind.

Andab. Etsi compositio in re alia sit quam quae in mente fit, non propterea effectum diversum existimo: cum si quem in mente habeat, eum ex ipsius rei natura habeat. Quare cum evidens sit ex compositione in mente contradictionem sequi, eandem etiam ex compositione in rerum natura necesse est intervenire. Constat itaque quicquid est, dum est, non posse non esse.

Andab. Although the composition in the thing be other than that which is made in the mind, not on that account do I judge [existimo] the effect diverse: since, if it [the composition] has any [effect] in the mind, it has it from the nature of the thing itself. Wherefore, since it is evident that from the composition in the mind a contradiction follows, it is necessary that the same [contradiction] also intervene from the composition in the nature of things. It stands [constat], therefore, that whatever is, while it is, cannot not-be.

Ereu. Verum idem antequam sit in eo signo, potest non esse in eodem signo, saltem quantum ex pura essentia seu Entis cum existentia complexione conficitur. Utrum enim ex causarum serie aliqua sit necessitas vel ex alia extrinseca lege, nihil molestus sim.

Ereu. But the same, before it be in that sign, can not-be in the same sign, at least so far as is effected [conficitur] from the pure essence, or [seu] from the complexion [complexione] of Being [Entis] with existence. For whether from the series of causes there be some necessity, or from another extrinsic law, I would be troublesome in nothing [nihil molestus sim].

Andab. Datum habes. Si quidem, ex eo quod potest interire, & aliquando natum est, & aliquando etiam non erit, clarum fit existentiae ad ens non esse adamantinam adhaesionem, & quod hinc fit, non aliam ex his terminis necessitatem esse praeterquam compositionis sive naturalis, sive mentalis, quarum nulla est rei pro illo signo, quo nondum pervenit.

Andab. You have [it] granted [Datum habes]. Since indeed, from this, that it can perish, and at some time was born, and at some time also will not be, it becomes clear that there is not an adamantine adhesion of existence to being [ens]; and, what comes [fit] from this, that there is no other necessity from these terms [terminis] besides [that] of composition, whether natural or mental, of which none belongs to the thing for that sign whither [quo] it has not yet arrived.

Ereu. Hoc itaque videor mihi ex dictis tuis palam conficere, nisi quid acutius discernas quam ego, successive corpori advenire τὸ non posse non esse, quantum ex connexione entis cum existentia illud habet.

Ereu. This, therefore, I seem to myself openly [palam] to conclude [conficere] from your sayings, unless you discern something more acutely than I: that to a body there comes successively [successive] the ‘not being able not to be’ [τὸ non posse non esse], so far as it has that from the connexion of being [entis] with existence.
Andab. Palam est.
Andab. It is open [Palam est].
Ereu. Ergo & hoc; successio aeterna cum non possit esse, neque corpus aliquod permanens aeternum esse posse: quoniam successive hoc ipsum accipere oporteat.
Ereu. Therefore this also: since an eternal succession cannot be, neither can any permanent body be eternal: since it must [oporteat] receive this very thing successively.

Andab. Asphali quid ais? Mihi enim aqua haeret: Hinc enim & deductorum claritudo, & quod concluso nescio qua propensione intus faveo, me cogit assentiri; Inde vero tum clarissimorum naturae Authorum reverentia, tum nescio quae nubes quam non satis explico, repellunt.

Andab. Asphalius, what do you say? For to me the water sticks [aqua haeret]: for on this side [Hinc] both the clearness [claritudo] of the things deduced, and that I favour the conclusion [concluso] within, by I know not what propension, compel [cogit] me to assent; on that side [Inde], however, both the reverence for the most famous [clarissimorum] Authors of nature, and I know not what cloud, which I do not sufficiently unfold [explico], repel [me].

Asphal. Me adhuc retinet quod si corpus sine motu conservatum aspicio, nescio qualis successio possit intelligi. Certe enim omnis realis successio motus est, si autem nulla est successio, signa & inclusa signis spatia nullo modo accipi possunt.

Asphal. Me this still holds back, that, if I look upon a body conserved without motion, I know not what kind of succession can be understood. For certainly all real succession is motion; but if there is no succession, signs [signa] and the spaces enclosed by signs can in no way be taken [accipi].

Andab. Oh quam verum est, quod aiunt otiosum spectatorem plus actore in ipsa ipsius actione perspicere! Hoc enim ipsum quod Asphalius proposuit, perturbatis in capite meo speciebus volutabatur, sed parere non valebam.

Andab. Oh how true it is, what they say, that the idle spectator perceives more than the actor in the very action of him [the actor]! For this very thing which Asphalius proposed was rolling about [volutabatur], the appearances [speciebus] in my head being disturbed, but I was not strong enough to bring [it] forth [parere].

Ereu. Et mihi contigit quod Deo accidisse fabulae Talmudicae narrant, litem aliquando de quaestione aliqua legis Deo contra populum intercidisse. Rabbinum quemdam doctissimum partes populi tutatum, productis legis verbis, causam adversus Deum evicisse: laetatumque Deum exclamavisse, filii mei vicerunt me. Nam haec ipsa difficultas quam vos tam facile dispexistis, me plures annos implicitum tenuit: tanquam firma demonstratione conclusum haberem: sed maiori video ad vos circuitione praeliandum. Agedum ergo, Andabata, quod de motu demonstratum est, credisne ad mutationes etiam pertinere? puta non posse esse mutationum infinitam successionem, sed ad unam perveniendum esse, qua non sit prior alia.

Ereu. To me also has happened what the Talmudic fables narrate to have befallen God: that a suit [litem] once arose [intercidisse] concerning some question of the law, for God against the people; that a certain most learned Rabbi, having protected the side [partes] of the people, the words of the law being brought forward, won [evicisse] the cause against God; and that God, rejoicing, exclaimed: ‘my sons have conquered me.’ For this very difficulty, which you so easily saw through [dispexistis], held me entangled [implicitum] for many [plures] years, as though I held [it] concluded by a firm demonstration; but I see [that] one must fight [praeliandum] against you with a greater circuit [circuitione]. Come then, Andabata, what has been demonstrated concerning motion, do you believe [that it] pertains also to changes [mutationes]? suppose [puta], that there cannot be an infinite succession of changes, but that one must arrive at one, than which there is not another prior.
Andab. Omnino, eodem enim Syllogismo mutatis tantummodo terminis debellatum erit. Si enim successio est infinita, inter duas aliquas, infinita continebitur succedentium multitudo.

Andab. Entirely; for by the same Syllogism, the terms [terminis] only being changed, it will have been fought out [debellatum erit]. For if the succession is infinite, between some two [changes] an infinite multitude of succeeding [things] will be contained.

terms: Archaic/poetic by-form of necesse est (Lucretius, Plautus); printed across the page break ‘neceſ-/ſum’.
Same sense; noted only because the form is unusual and could be misread as necessarium.
Instant, moment; ‘sign of nature’ (signum naturae) in scholastic usage is a logical rather than temporal priority.

White uses signum for a point of time (cf. glossary D3-N02); here ‘in signo praesenti’ = in the present instant. The argument trades on Aristotle’s principle that whatever is, while it is, necessarily is (De interpretatione 9, 19a23).
The argument from Dialogue I against an actual infinite: between any two determinate items only a finite number of intermediates can be enclosed.
‘Envious’ time: allusion to Horace, Odes I.11.7–8, ‘dum loquimur, fugerit invida / aetas’.
White echoes ‘dum loquimur’ in the parenthesis; invida agrees with an understood hora.
Grow dull / blunt / be at a loss.
Ironic: ‘I cannot see how’ = it is obvious it must be enclosed.
Scholastic ‘imaginary’ (non-real) time before creation, the counterpart of imaginary space (glossary: spatium imaginarium).
Andabata’s long-held opinion is the scholastic notion of a duration before the world; White denies real succession without motion.
Unusual word, possibly coined from placare; sense is clear from the medical image of swelling (tumor) subsiding.
composition in the thing / in the mind
Real union (of a subject with existence) vs. the mental composition of a proposition (subject + predicate).
Scholastic: truth of a proposition consists in the mind’s compositio answering to a compositio in re. Andabata argues the necessity ‘whatever is, while it is, cannot not-be’ holds of both.
Essence/existence distinction: from the bare essence no necessity of existing follows; cf. glossary complexio.
the ‘not being able not to be’
Greek article used to substantivise a Latin phrase, scholastic/humanist usage.
The necessity of the present (necessitas ex suppositione) accrues to a thing only successively, instant by instant—hence a permanent body would need an eternal succession.
Proverb = ‘I am stuck, at a loss’ (Cicero, De officiis III.117; Ad Q. fr. II.8).
the idle spectator perceives more than the actor
Proverb; cf. Seneca/Erasmus, ‘plus vident oculi quam oculus’; spectator vs actor in a play.
fabulae Talmudicae … filii mei vicerunt me
Talmudic fables … my sons have conquered me
Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 59b (‘oven of Akhnai’): God laughs and says ‘My sons have defeated me’ (nitzḥuni banai).
White’s retelling differs from the Talmud (there the dispute is between R. Eliezer and the sages, R. Joshua answers ‘it is not in heaven’). Example of 17th-c. Christian-Hebraist knowledge.
Roundabout way, detour; also a flanking march (military, with praeliandum).
Military metaphor: Ereunius must outflank his pupils with a longer argument.
Finish a war, vanquish; ‘it will have been settled’.
Continues the military metaphor; the same syllogism with changed terms (termini) defeats the infinite succession of changes.
Imperative of puto used adverbially = ‘for instance’, ‘that is to say’.
Introduces the restatement of the thesis.
notes: Unit: Dialogue III, Knot iii, complete. PDF pp. 296–300 = printed pp. 285–289, from Ereunius’ ‘Rem magnam postulas’ (p. 285; margin ‘Nodus III. Motum ab aeterno non extitisse’) to Andabata’s ‘…infinita continebitur succedentium multitudo.’ (p. 289). Knot iv begins on p. 289 with Ereunius’ ‘Haec itaque mutatio qua non est alia prior’ (margin ‘Nodus IV. Dari aliquod ab aeterno existens’). Offset +11 holds. Signatures: Nn iij (p. 285), Oo (p. 289).

Uncertain readings: (1) p. 285 ‘necessum est’ — printed ‘neceſ-’ at the foot of p. 285 and ‘ſum eſt’ at the head of p. 286; taken as the archaic necessum, not necesse. (2) p. 285 the first sentence states the opponent’s position (an infinite past motion), from which Ereunius draws the absurdity; ‘[on their view]’ is supplied. (3) p. 286 ‘in placorem’ — clear in print; a rare word. (4) p. 288 ‘parere’ printed with an accent-like mark (‘parêre’); read as parere ‘to bring forth’ (3rd conj.), which fits the birth image; ‘parēre’ (to obey/appear) gives no sense. (5) p. 289 ‘tanquam firma demonstratione conclusum haberem’ — sense ambiguous: either the difficulty kept Ereunius entangled even though he thought he had his thesis demonstrated, or he was held as though bound by a firm demonstration; translated literally. (6) p. 287 ‘τὸ’ — the Greek article is printed (‘τὸ’ with grave accent), transcribed as such.

Verification pass (Latin re-read against page images and English sentence by sentence): 5 corrections. (1) p. 286 ‘cum si quem in mente habeat’ — the subject supplied as ‘[the composition]’, not ‘[the mental one]’; quem = aliquem effectum. (2) ‘potest non esse’ / ‘non posse non esse’ rendered ‘can not-be’ / ‘cannot not-be’ to keep the modal scope distinct from ‘cannot be’. (3) p. 288 ablative absolute ‘perturbatis … speciebus’ rendered literally (‘the appearances … being disturbed’) instead of as a prepositional phrase. (4) p. 288 ‘partes populi tutatum’ — ‘partes’ rendered ‘side [partes]’ (role in a suit) not ‘part’. (5) p. 288 ‘me cogit’ is singular with two subjects; English ‘compel [cogit]’ keeps the Latin in brackets so the agreement is visible. Nothing found omitted or added.

Conventions: as in glossary.md — nodus = Knot; signum (of time) = sign [signo]; consonantal u → v, long s → s, æ → ae, accents dropped; supplied words in [square brackets]; marginal note given as its own row at the start.
